extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Māori culture and New Zealand history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and factual background for representing Māori social structures, beliefs, history and practices accurately in creative or interpretive writing. Useful for authors aiming to portray Māori land relationships, gender roles, rituals, leadership and material culture with cultural and historical nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Māori relationship with the land (mana and whakapapa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Māori relationship with the land is complex. Traditionally the resources the land held were controlled based on systems of mana (power) and whakapapa (ancestral right). The land itself was both sacred and abstract. In many cases multiple groups would express a connection with the same important river or mountain. Oral tradition would record the migrations of groups from one area to another and their connection with an ancestral location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying land and place, indicate collective, ancestral and sacred connections rather than purely individual ownership. Represent overlapping group rights, ancestral ties and spiritual dimensions of landscape; avoid reducing relationships to simple freehold/private-property models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'tuku' and early land deals
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been argued that the use of the word tuku in deeds, meaning to let or allow or give freely, was not the same as selling. This and other interpretations of early 19th century New Zealand land deals have been the source of much disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray early transactions with nuance: deeds signed with Māori were often conditional or limited rather than equivalent to British freehold sale. Avoid depicting early sales as straightforward transfers of permanent individual title if the historical context suggests otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of European trade and money adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: With the arrival of Europeans Māori gradually started to trust the value of British money and use it as a medium of exchange instead of goods. By 1839 a large proportion of the Māori trade in goods was paid for in cash, with Māori showing a strong preference for coins rather than paper banknotes. Northern Māori learnt that they could more easily hide cash from their relatives avoiding the traditional obligatory sharing of goods with their hapū.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about economic change, show how cash and new trade practices altered social behaviours (e.g., accumulation, secrecy, shifting obligations) and power relations within hapū and between chiefs and families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade increasing chiefs' influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of trading increased the influence of chiefs over their hapū. Northern traders assumed that the chief was the organisational head of the hapū and all trade went through him including payments for goods purchased. This gave chiefs much more influence, especially after 1835, because trade was so regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect how regular trade amplified chiefly authority compared with pre-contact consensus decision-making; character interactions and social dynamics should show this shift rather than assuming static pre-colonial hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Māori maritime commerce and investment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1850s ... Māori with the active encouragement of Grey embraced trade were gradually able to develop a large fleet of small trading schooners and similar craft. Māori paid customs duties to the government and invested heavily in vessels, so suffered considerably when a dramatic market slump hit New Zealand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include Māori agency in maritime trade and commerce—ownership, investment, and the economic risks they bore—rather than treating shipping and trade as solely European enterprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Lands Act and individualisation of title
rubrics_metrics.description: The Native Lands Act was a policy enforced by the government in 1865, which allowed the Māori people to obtain individual titles for their land to sell. This act abolished the traditional shared landholdings and made it easier for European settlers to directly purchase land for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exploring land loss in narratives, show the legal and social mechanisms (e.g., Native Lands Acts, court processes) that transformed communal landholding into alienable individual title, and the resulting social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marae protocol and pōwhiri
rubrics_metrics.description: References and links to 'What is a Marae?', 'Pōwhiri Process' and 'Marae protocol – te kawa o te marae' indicate formal protocols for welcome and proceedings on the marae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depictions of marae and pōwhiri should respect and reflect established protocols (karanga, whaikōrero, hongi, etc.). Avoid inventing or misrepresenting ceremonial sequences; consult sources or local kawa for accurate ceremonial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tapu and noa and women's mediating roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Women have roles that help mediate between tapu and noa, resulting in strong connections between life and death. This can be represented by women helping with pregnancies and childbirth, as well as being kaikaranga who call to mourners before tangihanga. These roles are perceived as better suited for women rather than men due to their spiritual connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent women's spiritual roles (kaikaranga, childbirth-related rituals, mourning callers) as important and respected functions within tikanga; avoid marginalising these roles or casting them solely as domestic duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender roles flexible pre-colonially
rubrics_metrics.description: In recent times, diversity of roles among men and women is more equal. Nevertheless, many believe that pre-colonial Māori society did not have set roles based on gender. Instead, people worked as a group to carry out tasks, such as gathering food. Women participated in many male dominant duties, such as healers and religious leaders, although not everyone supported it. This varies across different iwi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about gender in historical settings, avoid imposing rigid European gender binaries; allow for role-fluidity and regional/iwi variation, and show that gendered divisions of labour were not uniform across Māori societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: European missionary influence on gender and tapu
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1800s, European missionaries spread Christianity ... Tapu and noa were combined with Christian ideas in order to show women as sinful and destructive. One example of this is menstruation - once seen as tapu, Christian influence considered it negative and unclean. Women’s roles in society changed, giving them less power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray colonial and missionary influences as changing gendered meanings (e.g., reframing of tapu practices) and diminishing some women's roles; show cultural transformation rather than assuming static traditional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whakapapa and identity formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Men’s identity is formed through affiliation with others, heritage, and their own wellbeing. Whakapapa connects Māori to their ancestors, land, and spiritual world. For many Māori men there is a strong focus on heritage in relation to their geographic location. For example, their identities are stronger when they are living where their ancestors lived and raising children that will grow strong alongside their ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character motivations and identities should reference whakapapa and place-based belonging; ancestral linkage and continuity with land are central identity elements to reflect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingitanga (Māori King movement) as political strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The kotahitanga or unity movement ... promoted idea of forming a Māori kingdom, with one king ruling over all tribes. The King movement came to have a flag, a council of state, a code of laws, a 'King's Resident Magistrate', police, a bank, a surveyor and a newspaper, all of which gave the movement the appearance of an alternative government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depictions of Māori political movements should show organizational sophistication (institutions, symbols, legal codes) and motivations (unity, equal standing with the Crown) rather than simplifying them as purely symbolic or reactionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warfare and military participation
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Classic period warfare was an important part of Māori culture. This continued through the contact period and was expressed during the 20th century by large groups of volunteers in the First and Second world wars. The Māori Battalion in North Africa (1941) is a well known example of Māori involvement in New Zealand's military.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including conflict or military themes, acknowledge both traditional warfare practices and later forms of military service; avoid romanticising or stereotyping aggression and note social/political contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tikanga, kaitiakitanga and cultural values
rubrics_metrics.description: References to 'Tikanga Māori: Living by Māori values' and 'Kaitiakitanga – guardianship and conservation' point to tikanga and guardianship as central values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narratives, integrate tikanga principles (proper behaviour, guardianship of resources, reciprocity) as lived cultural logic shaping decisions and relationships rather than mere background detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material culture and artistic practices (moko, carving, weaving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentions of moko, revival of ta moko, whakairo (carving), korowai cloaks, uhi (chisels), and other art forms show the importance of material and visual culture in Māori life and revival movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe material culture (tattooing, carving, cloaks, weaving) with attention to technique, social meaning and contemporary revivals; avoid appropriation or inaccurate visual detail, and consult specialists or iwi sources for precise descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and presence of te reo Māori
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as Te Peeke o Aotearoa banknotes with Māori text and numerous Māori terms throughout the page (e.g., hapū, iwi, marae, pōwhiri) demonstrate the presence and importance of te reo Māori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate te reo Māori selectively and accurately; use correct terms for social units and ceremonies, and consider providing context for non-Māori readers. Avoid tokenistic or incorrect usage.
